how-long-does-dns-propagation-take.html.text:
How long does DNS propagation take?

Short answer: it is not a journey, so nothing is travelling. A change is live at your provider immediately, and the wait you are feeling is other people's resolvers holding a cached copy of the old answer until its TTL runs out.

What sets the wait

Three things, in the order they usually bite:

  1. The old record's TTL. A resolver that cached the previous answer keeps serving it for as long as the TTL it received. That is the number that bounds an ordinary record edit.
  2. Whether the nameservers changed. A delegation change is resolved through the TLD zone, whose TTLs run to days, which is where the folklore figure of 24 to 48 hours comes from.
  3. Resolver behaviour. Some resolvers clamp very short TTLs upward, so a 60-second TTL does not guarantee a 60-second wait everywhere.

None of these are visible from a provider panel, which is why a change can look finished to you and not to a customer.

How to plan a cutover around it

  1. Lower the TTL on the records you are about to change, well before the change window.
  2. Wait at least the old TTL, so resolvers have picked up the shorter one.
  3. Record what named resolvers answer now — this is your before.
  4. Make the change.
  5. Record the same queries again, and compare. What is still unchanged is what is still cached.

Questions

How long does DNS propagation actually take?

There is no propagation event to wait for. An authoritative change is live the moment your DNS provider publishes it. What you are actually waiting on is every recursive resolver that already holds the old answer in cache, and each one keeps it until the TTL it was handed expires. So the honest upper bound is the TTL that was on the old record when a resolver last looked it up, not a fixed number of hours.

Why does everyone say 24 to 48 hours?

That figure comes from changing which nameservers a domain uses, not from editing a record. A delegation change has to be picked up through the TLD zone, whose TTLs are measured in days rather than minutes, and some resolvers hold a delegation longer still. Editing an A, MX or TXT record while the nameservers stay put is usually bounded by that record's own TTL instead, which is often an hour or less.

Can I make a change go faster once I have already made it?

No. Once resolvers have cached the old answer, nothing done at the authoritative side shortens the TTL they were already given. Speed has to be arranged beforehand: lower the TTL on the record, wait for the old TTL to expire so resolvers pick up the shorter one, and only then make the real change. After the fact the only options are waiting, and being able to show what has moved so far.

How do I know the change is actually done?

By asking named resolvers and writing down what they answered, rather than trusting a provider panel that shows intent rather than effect. Capture what a set of resolvers answer before the change, capture the same queries again afterwards, and compare the two. During the window different resolvers will legitimately disagree, and a per-resolver record shows that instead of averaging it away.

Does this tool show me the TTL?

No. It records the answers each resolver returned and compares them; it does not record the TTL attached to those answers. Read the TTL from your DNS provider's panel, or from a dig query, if you need to predict how long the wait will be. This tool is for establishing what changed, not for forecasting when it will.

Why does one online propagation checker say done and another say not yet?

Because they queried different resolvers, at different moments, from different places. That is the normal shape of a change still in flight, not a fault in either checker. It is also why a single global verdict is the least useful thing such a tool can report, and why this one keeps every resolver on its own row.

Want the before-and-after record? DNS Change Evidence captures what Cloudflare, Google and Quad9 answer for a domain, then compares two captures and reports changed, unchanged and inconclusive separately. It runs entirely in your browser, and it is free. Already using a worldwide checker like whatsmydns.net for the "has it spread yet" view? See how the two compare.

No warranty. This page is free and as-is, and it is general operational explanation rather than DNS, security, deliverability, compliance, legal, or professional advice. TTL behaviour varies between resolvers and providers, so treat the timings here as how the mechanism works rather than a guarantee about your domain. You are responsible for confirming your authorization to change or query a domain, and for reviewing any record before relying on it. The authors accept no liability for loss or damage arising from its use.

What did that DNS change actually do?

Capture what public resolvers answer for a customer domain now, make your change, then capture again. You get a dated, source-linked record of what changed, what did not, and what could not be observed at all.

After using this, you can now hand a customer evidence that a nameserver move or a mail cutover did what you said it would — instead of a screenshot of a control panel, which shows what you asked for rather than what the internet answers.

Free, no account, no server of ours. The lookups are made by your own browser over DNS-over-HTTPS.

Step 1

Capture a snapshot

Run this once before your change, and again after it.

Every name queried must sit inside this domain. That scope is the tool’s authorization boundary.

Supported types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, TXT, SOA, CAA, SRV, PTR.

Resolvers

Each is recorded separately, so partial propagation is visible rather than averaged away.

Latest capture

NameTypeResolverAnswer
Step 2

Compare before and after

The “after” is your latest capture above. Give it a “before” to compare against.

Before

Nothing loaded yet.

After

Nothing captured yet.

Evidence report

    NameTypeResolverResultBeforeAfter

    What this does not do

    It does not write DNS records, send mail, test uptime, monitor continuously, or judge whether a configuration is correct, secure, or deliverable. It records what named resolvers answered at two moments and states the difference between them. Whether a difference matters is your call.

    Inconclusive is not “no change”. A timeout, a refusal, or a query asked in only one of the two captures is reported as inconclusive and counted separately. It is never folded into the unchanged total.

    Questions

    What problem does this solve?

    After a nameserver move, a mail provider switch, or a TXT record edit, somebody has to be able to say what actually changed. Screenshots of a DNS panel show intent, not effect, and a green tick from a monitoring tool shows the current state without the state it replaced. This captures what named public resolvers answered before the change and again after it, and reports the difference as a record you can keep or hand to a customer.

    Does my domain list leave my browser?

    There is no account, no server of ours, and no analytics vendor. The DNS lookups are made by your own browser directly to the public DNS-over-HTTPS endpoints you tick — Cloudflare, Google and Quad9 — exactly as any web request from your machine would be. Those resolvers see the query, as they would if you simply visited the domain. Nothing is sent to us, because there is nothing of ours in the path. Snapshots stay in your browser until you download them.

    Why does it report 'inconclusive' instead of 'no change'?

    Because they are different claims, and conflating them is how an evidence tool becomes worthless. If a resolver timed out, refused the query, or was not asked the same question in both captures, the honest statement is that nothing was observed — not that nothing changed. Inconclusive findings are counted and listed separately, and they are never folded into the unchanged total.

    Is this a DNS monitoring or security tool?

    No. It does not write records, send mail, test uptime, watch continuously, or judge whether a configuration is correct or secure. It records what specific resolvers answered at two moments and states the difference. Deciding whether a difference matters is the operator's job.

    Why query three resolvers instead of one?

    Propagation is the usual reason a DNS change looks done to one person and not to another. Recording each resolver separately makes that visible: a change that has landed at Cloudflare and not yet at Google shows as changed on one row and unchanged on another, which is the actual situation rather than an average of it.

    Can I use this with the command-line version?

    Yes. The snapshot JSON this page downloads is the same schema the Python package in the repository reads, so a baseline captured here can be compared with python3 -m dns_evidence compare, and a snapshot captured by the CLI can be loaded here as the 'before'. The two produce the same report.

    Why does a CNAME'd name show no A record?

    Only the record type you asked for is recorded, so a CNAME in the resolution chain is never written down as if it were the A record. Query CNAME on that name to see the chain itself.

    Still waiting on a change to land? How long does DNS propagation take? covers what actually sets the wait, and how to plan a cutover around it.

    Wondering how this compares to a global propagation checker like whatsmydns.net? See this tool vs. whatsmydns.net.

    One caveat when mixing the browser and the CLI

    The CLI queries resolvers directly over the DNS protocol; this page goes through DNS-over-HTTPS, and those endpoints present record text with small cosmetic differences (trailing dots, TXT quoting). This page normalises what it receives, so two captures made here always compare cleanly. Mixing a CLI capture with a browser capture can show a cosmetic “changed” on a record that did not really move. Capture both halves the same way and the question does not arise.

    No warranty. This tool is free and as-is. It is an operational observation record, not a DNS, security, deliverability, or compliance authority, and it is not legal or professional advice. It does not establish global DNS truth — only what the resolvers you selected answered at the moments you ran it. You are responsible for confirming your authorization to query a domain, for reviewing the record before relying on or sharing it, and for deciding whether any difference needs action. The authors accept no liability for loss or damage arising from its use.

    Free and open source. If it confirmed a DNS change went where you expected, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

    Keeping the same kind of record for backups? The backup verification evidence tool reads run records in your browser and shows whether last night's archive shrank or a verified job quietly got worse.

    Checking a specific set of DNS records rather than diffing a change over time? The email authentication checker reads a domain's SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and BIMI records and reports what each one means for spoofing and deliverability — a point-in-time evidence read of one specific record family, next to this tool's before/after diff of whatever records you name.

vs-whatsmydns.html.text:
← DNS Change Evidence

This tool vs. whatsmydns.net

whatsmydns.net shows one worldwide snapshot right now: what a network of resolvers in many countries currently answer for a domain. This tool captures two dated snapshots — before your change and after it — and reports what moved, what did not, and what could not be observed at all.

What each tool is for

whatsmydns.net is a free, no-account web tool built for one question: has a DNS change reached different parts of the world yet? Enter a domain and a record type, and it queries a network of DNS resolvers located in many different countries at once, showing what each currently answers. That single live view is exactly what it is for, and it does it well. It keeps no history between visits — there is nothing to compare a later look against, and nothing you can hand someone as a dated record of what a resolver answered an hour ago.

This tool does the other half. It captures what named resolvers answer for a domain now, lets you make your change, captures again afterward, and diffs the two captures into a report that keeps changed, unchanged, and inconclusive separate — a timeout or a refused query is never folded into "no change". That report is a file you keep or hand to a customer, source-linked to the exact resolvers and timestamps behind it. It runs free in your browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type; a matching Python CLI lets you name a specific resolver, such as a customer's internal one, that a browser cannot reach.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Has this change reached different regions of the world yet?whatsmydns.net, or a comparable global propagation checker.
I need a dated, source-linked record of what changed for a customer or a handover note.This tool — free, no account.
I want a distinct "could not be observed" state, not a timeout silently read as "unchanged".This tool's inconclusive finding.
I just want a quick worldwide look right now, no capture-then-recapture workflow.whatsmydns.net.
I need to query a specific resolver I name myself, such as a customer's internal one.This tool's command-line version.
Why does a change look done from one location and not another?This tool's own propagation walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?Neither tool requires one.

Most DNS cutovers get value from both, at different points in the same change: whatsmydns.net (or a comparable global checker) for a quick sense of how far a change has spread across the world, and this tool for the dated, resolver-by-resolver record that says exactly what a specific set of resolvers answered before and after — the record a customer, a ticket, or an audit actually needs to keep. Neither tool decides whether a difference matters; that judgement stays with whoever is running the change.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, every capture runs in your own browser over DNS-over-HTTPS, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Should I use this tool or whatsmydns.net?

They answer different questions, and a DNS cutover usually needs both. whatsmydns.net is a free, no-account web tool: enter a domain and a record type, and it queries a network of DNS resolvers located in many different countries at once, showing what each one currently answers right now. It is built for one question — has a change reached different parts of the world yet — and it answers that well as a single live snapshot. It keeps no history between visits and produces nothing you can save as a dated record: refresh the page tomorrow and today's view is gone. This tool does the opposite half of the job. It captures what named resolvers answer now, lets you make your change, captures again afterward, and diffs the two into a report that states changed, unchanged, and inconclusive separately rather than folding a timeout into 'no change'. That report is a file you keep or hand to a customer, not a page you have to remember to screenshot. It runs free in your browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A cutover that needs to know how far a change has spread geographically is a job for whatsmydns.net or a comparable global checker; a cutover that needs a dated, source-linked record of what actually moved is a job for this tool.

Does this tool check the same worldwide network of locations as whatsmydns.net?

No, and it is not trying to. The browser surface here queries three named public resolvers — Cloudflare, Google, and Quad9 — over DNS-over-HTTPS, and the command-line version can query any resolver you name yourself, such as a customer's internal one. Neither is a stand-in for a network of resolvers spread across many countries, which is what a global propagation checker like whatsmydns.net is built for. If what you need to know is whether a change has reached many different regions of the world, use a global checker for that view. If what you need is a comparable, dated answer from a specific handful of resolvers — before the change and after it — that is what this tool records.

Is this page affiliated with whatsmydns.net?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by whatsmydns.net or its operators. whatsmydns.net is named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, and no claim is made about it beyond its well-documented category: a free, no-account, global DNS propagation checker.

Open DNS Change Evidence to capture a before/after record for your own domain.

No warranty. This tool is free and as-is. It is an operational observation record, not a DNS, security, deliverability, or compliance authority, and it is not legal or professional advice. It does not establish global DNS truth — only what the resolvers you selected answered at the moments you ran it. You are responsible for confirming your authorization to query a domain, for reviewing the record before relying on or sharing it, and for deciding whether any difference needs action. The authors accept no liability for loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every capture stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against whatsmydns.net — it is a static page describing a publicly documented category of tool.
